posts.title: Write the rule as a hook, not a sentence
posts.linkedin:
I told my AI agents, in writing, never to commit in the shared checkout.

Several of them work against the same repos at once, and the shared checkout can hold another agent's uncommitted work at any moment. One stray commit there sweeps it into the wrong branch.

The fix wasn't a better sentence. It was a hook that blocks the command. Now an agent that tries gets a BLOCKED message and a pointer to take its own git worktree.

Rules a model is supposed to remember are suggestions. Rules the harness enforces are rules.

posts.title: How I write architecture decision records
posts.visual: Screenshot of one short ADR with title, context, decision and consequences visible (pick one with no customer names, e.g. "time bookings are an append-only ledger")
posts.linkedin:
There are about 50 architecture decision records across the three platforms I build. Most are under a page.

How I write them:

One decision per record. The title is the decision, not the topic. "No email sends without human approval" beats "Email strategy".

Context in a paragraph. What forced the decision now.

The alternative I rejected, and why. This is the part future me actually reads. Without it, every ADR looks obvious and every reversal looks reasonable.

Consequences, including the bad ones. An append-only time ledger means corrections are new entries, not edits. That's more rows and a slightly odder UI. Written down, so nobody "fixes" it later.

Written before the code, or at the latest in the same PR.

Why bother on a team of one? Because I'm not really a team of one. I work with AI coding agents, and an agent has no memory of why the schema looks the way it does. The ADRs are how it finds out. A decision that isn't written down gets quietly re-made by the next session that touches the code.

Do you keep ADRs? What's the one section you'd never drop?

posts.title: Packing for a travelling wetlab: before and after
posts.visual: Two-panel image: left, a paper packing checklist (stock photo or mock-up, no real data); right, the live packing screen with dummy data
posts.linkedin:
Before: packing for a travelling wetlab event meant paper lists and tribal knowledge. What goes in which crate for which course depended on who had packed it last time.

After:

Courses are planned as rooms → stations → equipment.

Packing lists are generated from templates per session. Deterministic: same course, same list.

A live packing screen over WebSockets lets several people work the same checklist at once and see each other's ticks.

Serialised equipment is tracked. Vehicle capacity is known before the van is loaded.

This started as a small tool, WetPack, in February. It's now part of the operations platform I'm building in Django, alongside bookings, staffing and certificates.

The lesson: the paper list wasn't the problem. The problem was that the knowledge of what goes on it lived in people. Templates moved it into the system.

posts.title: Small trained model or general LLM?
posts.linkedin:
Genuine question for people running AI in production.

For segmenting surgical training videos into procedure phases, I had two options:

A. A general vision-language model (Qwen3-VL, self-hosted via Ollama). Ask it what phase it's looking at.

B. A small supervised model (a frozen image encoder under an MS-TCN++ temporal model), trained locally, judged against a locked test set.

I went with B as the default and kept A as opt-in. A gives plausible answers. B gives a number I can defend, and I know when it gets worse.

But B costs labelled data and training time, and A gets better every few months without me doing anything.

Where do you draw that line? At what point would you switch back to the general model?

posts.title: Project reveal: a second brain that agents maintain
posts.visual: Diagram: voice note (Telegram) → self-hosted speech-to-text → transcript → agent extracts concepts → Markdown vault → 3D graph view, with GitHub issues as satellite nodes. No screenshot exists yet; draw the diagram, or capture the graph with dummy concepts.
posts.linkedin:
Something I've been building on the side of the day job: a second brain that agents maintain for me.

The loop:

I send a voice note on Telegram.
A self-hosted speech-to-text service transcribes it.
An agent pulls out the concepts and links them into a Markdown vault: products, capabilities, offers, ideas, with typed relations between them.
A read-only 3D graph app lays the vault out (UMAP) so I can see what connects to what. Open GitHub issues show up as satellite nodes on the concepts they belong to.

Claude Code reads and writes the vault over MCP, so the same knowledge is there when I'm planning work.

Two decisions made it work. The domain language (Vault, Concept, Utterance) was written down before any code. And the graph app is strictly a read-only consumer. Only one thing writes to the vault, so the vault stays the truth.

It's small: 18 commits, five ADRs.

posts.title: Downhill skateboarding taught me my first Django app
posts.visual: A photo of you skating (or a road you skate near Innsbruck), no faces of others without consent
posts.linkedin:
My first real Django app wasn't for work. It was for downhill skateboarding.

[VERIFY: the itch, e.g. events scattered across group chats.] So in December 2024 I started an events calendar: profiles, comments and reviews, filtering, email reminders. About 120 commits later it's still going.

Everything I now do at work started there. Models that match how people actually talk about the thing. An admin someone else can use. Email that goes out when it should, and only then.

Moving from Dublin to Innsbruck [VERIFY: when you moved] was partly about the work and partly about the hills. There are a lot more of them here.

The lesson I keep relearning: build the thing you'd use yourself first. You find out fast what's annoying.

posts.title: Nothing AI-written reaches a person without a human
posts.linkedin:
One rule shows up in every platform I build: nothing generated reaches a real person without a human approving it.

In the operations platform, it's a decision record: no email sends without human approval. In the content tool, AI drafts and a person approves by email before anything ships.

It costs a click. It buys you every mistake caught before it's someone else's problem.

Self-hosting the model keeps the data in. The approval step keeps the errors in.

posts.title: How my agents hand over at the end of a shift
posts.visual: Screenshot of a sample handover report with a dummy project (sections: what works, what's verified, what's next)
posts.linkedin:
My AI agents have shift changes. It sounds silly. It fixed the most annoying problem I had.

The problem: a new session starts with no memory. It re-reads half the repo to work out where things stand, then confidently trusts a TODO comment from three weeks ago.

So there are two protocols, written as skills.

End of shift:
Clean the repo. No stray branches, no half-staged files.
Verify what actually works. Run it. Don't infer it from the code.
Sync the docs to reality.
Leave a written health report the next engineer, human or agent, can act on without this conversation.

Start of shift:
Rebuild context from the repository alone.
Check the handover's claims against reality, not the other way round.
Surface what moved since: merges, new issues, failed CI.
Recommend the first task.

The rule that makes it work: the repo is the memory. Not the chat. If it isn't committed or written down in the repo, the next shift doesn't know it.

A hook also re-injects the current repo, branch and PR state when a session resumes, so agents don't burn turns re-orienting.

posts.title: Course feedback: from paper forms to PDF reports
posts.visual: A sample generated PDF report page with dummy data, showing one server-rendered chart
posts.linkedin:
Before: course feedback at medical congresses meant paper forms, then someone typing them in, then someone building a report.

After:

Each session gets a QR code. Participants scan it and answer on their phone. No login.

Results show up on a live dashboard while the event is still running.

Sessions get benchmark percentiles against each other.

At the end, session and event-level PDF reports are generated automatically, with the event's branding. Charts are rendered server-side with matplotlib straight into the PDF via ReportLab. Export to CSV and Excel for anyone who wants the raw numbers.

Small Django app, 26 commits, now being folded into the main operations platform.

The bit people don't expect: server-side charts. No headless browser, no screenshot step. The PDF is the same every time.

posts.title: Erasing a person, keeping their certificate
posts.linkedin:
GDPR erasure gets interesting when the data is meant to be public.

Our certificates have public verification pages. Anyone can check that a certificate is real.

So when someone asks to be erased, deleting the row isn't right, and keeping it isn't either.

What we do: scrub the name and personal data, keep the credential. The page still says "valid certificate". It no longer says whose.

Privacy rules belong in the model, not in a policy PDF.

posts.title: What's your review budget?
posts.linkedin:
Question for anyone using AI agents for code review.

I ran one 92-file PR through three rounds of adversarial review: one agent tries to break it, a judge on a different, stronger model rules on each finding. Every round found new major issues.

It wasn't converging. There was just too much surface.

So now review has a budget. PRs are capped in size. One reviewer by default. At most two fix rounds, and round two only looks at the fix. Whatever's left becomes an issue.

It feels like giving up. In practice, review now ends.

Do you cap review? By rounds, by PR size, by time? Or do you let it run until it's clean?

posts.title: From a trip-cost splitter to a platform
posts.visual: Side-by-side: an early public project's README or screenshot (e.g. tournament-brackets) next to an architecture sketch of the current platform with no client names
posts.linkedin:
November 2023: I wrote my first HTML and CSS page.

February 2024: a JavaScript app that splits the cost of a trip between friends.

March 2024: a Python CLI for knockout tournament brackets.

December 2026: I'm the engineer on a Django operations platform with 6000+ tests, a surgical video platform live at congresses, and a team of AI agents I run with written rules and enforced hooks.

What got me from one to the other wasn't talent. It was building in public, small and often, and writing down why I made each decision. Most of those early projects are still public on my GitHub. They're rough. I leave them up on purpose.

If you're early in this and wondering whether the walkthrough projects matter: they do. Not because anyone reads them, but because you did them.

What did you build first?
